newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya airport strike may cost 'millions'- Lufthansa.
newsitem.headline: Kenya airport strike may cost 'millions'- Lufthansa.

text.p: Lufthansa Cargo on Monday said a strike currently crippling all Kenya's airports could cost the air cargo industry here "millions of dollars" if it continued must longer.

At the same time air traffic controllers at the international airport in Nairobi said they planned to increase delays on flights from Tuesday and were determined to continue until the government met their demands.

"So far we have not heard anything from the government and we are in fact trying to increase flight delays," said one air traffic controller, who wished to remain anonymous, told Reuters. "Right now we are delaying flights by at least an hour, but we are planning to double the delay."

The strike, which began at midnight on Friday in both Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and Moi International Airport in Mombasa, the country's second city and centre of Kenya's tourist industry, continued throughout Monday with demands for better pay and working conditions.
"This time we are determined to continue the strike until we get what we want," the controller said.

Lufthansa Cargo and freight forwarders earlier on Monday called for urgent action from the government to find a solution on the strike which continued to cause major delays to air cargo and passenger traffic.
"I think this is disastrous," David Keary, general manager for Lufthansa Cargo in East and Central Africa told Reuters.

"An airline industry is very sensitive to such things. It's not just this one flight here which is delayed, it's flights in the whole system which get delayed and if this goes on much longer...it could cost millions (of dollars)."

He said since the perishable goods industry accounted for some 90 percent of all Kenya's air freight, the loss of customers due to unreliable delivery could be a severe blow to air cargo as well as the horticulture industry.
"The air cargo here is mostly based on perishable goods and if you took it away it would be the death of the air cargo industry," Keary said.

"If this continues much longer we will have to look around for other places to fill up our freighters, we can't sit around and wait for the Kenyan government to sort out their problems with the air traffic controllers."
Lufthansa Cargo said the majority of all their weekend Frankfurt-bound perishable cargo had been delayed more than 24 hours by the strike.

Airlink, an 85 percent-owned subsidiary of Swiss freight forwarders Kuehne & Nagel, said late Monday it was close to writing-off five tonnes of fresh cut flowers, which have awaited flight connection to Johannesburg since Saturday.
Airlink was scheduled to fly that particular flower load to Johannesburg Saturday morning, but due to the go-slow the flight was cancelled and by Monday evening the cargo had still not left Nairobi.
"This is a major problem. All of it is perishable cargo which was going to Johannesburg with a lot of it bound for connecting flights to Taipei and Australia," an Airlink spokesman said.
"It's very bad for the flowers, we have more or the less lost it," he said.
